'''Siegfried S. Hecker''' (born October 2, 1943) is an American [[metallurgical engineer|metallurgist]] and [[nuclear scientist]]. He served as Director of [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/the-american-scientist-whos-seen-north-korea-nuclear-secrets/|title=The American scientist who's seen North Korea's nuclear secrets|access-date=2018-01-28|language=en}}</ref> from 1986 to 1997 and is now affiliated with [[Stanford University]], where he is research professor emeritus in the Department of Management Science and Engineering in the School of Engineering, and senior fellow emeritus at the [[Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://cisac.fsi.stanford.edu/people/siegfried_s_hecker|title=FSI {{!}} CISAC - Siegfried S. Hecker|website=cisac.fsi.stanford.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-01-28}}</ref> During this time, he was also elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (1988) for outstanding research on plutonium and the forming of materials, and for leadership in developing energy and weapons systems.

==Biography==
===Early life===
Hecker's parents came from [[Sarajevo]], Bosnia, and were moved during World War II to [[Tomaszew, Masovian Voivodeship|Tomaszew]], [[Poland]], where Hecker was born.<ref name=reflections>{{cite web | url=http://www.lanl.gov/news/reflections/0897.pdf  |author=LA National Laboratory |title=Reflections (Issue about S. Hecker) |page=16 |date=August–September 1997 |accessdate=November 23, 2010}}</ref> When his father had not returned from the war at the [[Eastern Front (World War II)|Eastern Front]], his mother remarried and settled in [[Rottenmann]], Austria.<ref name=reflections/> The family emigrated from [[Styria]] to the US in 1956.

===Education===
Hecker completed his [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[Metallurgy]] in 1965, his [[Master of Science]] in Metallurgy in 1967, and his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in [[Metallurgical Engineering]] in 1968, all from [[Case Western Reserve University]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nae.edu/119547.aspx|title=Siegfried S. Hecker Biography|website=NAE Website|access-date=2018-01-28}}</ref> He then spent two years as a postdoctoral appointee at the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]].

===Professional career===
Hecker began his professional career as a senior research metallurgist with the [[General Motors Research Laboratories]] in 1970.

===Los Alamos===
[[File:Siegfried S. Hecker.jpg|thumb|upright=0.6|Hecker while director of Los Alamos National Laboratory]]
After Hecker's return to the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], he led the laboratory's Materials Science and Technology Division and Center for Materials Science.<ref name=":0" /> He then served as the fifth Director of the Los Alamos National Laboratory from 1986 till 1997 and was a Los Alamos Senior Fellow until 2005.<ref name=":0" />

===Stanford University===
He first came to [[Stanford University]] as a visiting professor in 2005. In 2007 he became co-director of the [[Stanford University Center for International Security and Cooperation]] (CISAC) in the [[Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies]] and held this post until 2012.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://daily.stanford.edu/article/2007/2/16/heckerWillCodirectCisac |title=Hecker will co-direct CISAC |date=February 16, 2007 |author=Mahncy Mehrotra |work=The Stanford Daily |accessdate=2008-09-24 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070218223314/http://daily.stanford.edu/article/2007/2/16/heckerWillCodirectCisac |archivedate=February 18, 2007 }}</ref><ref name=P-20130227>{{cite news |url=http://fsi-ws1.stanford.edu/news/hecker_steps_down_as_codirector_but_not_away_from_cisac_20130227/ |title=Hecker steps down as co-director, but not away from CISAC |author=Beth Duff-Brown |newspaper=FSI Stanford News |date=27 February 2013 |accessdate=16 July 2015 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150716163546/http://fsi-ws1.stanford.edu/news/hecker_steps_down_as_codirector_but_not_away_from_cisac_20130227/ |archivedate=16 July 2015 }}</ref>

===Other activities===
====Nuclear Threat Initiative====
Hecker also acts as advisor to the [[Nuclear Threat Initiative]] board of directors and belongs to the advisory council of [[CRDF Global]], an independent nonprofit organization that promotes international scientific and technical collaboration.

====Visits to North Korea====
[[File:Yongbyon, disabled nuclear fuel fabrication facility.jpg|thumb|Hecker visiting the disabled Yongbyon Nuclear Scientific Research Center, North Korea, in 2008]]
He has visited [[North Korea]] frequently in an unofficial capacity to assess the plutonium program at the [[Yongbyon Nuclear Scientific Research Center]] (once every year since 2004).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.fas.org/irp/congress/2004_hr/012104hecker.pdf|title=Visit to the Yongbyon Nuclear Scientific Research Center in North Korea|author=Siegfried S. Hecker|date=21 January 2004|id=LA-UR-04-0340|accessdate=2008-09-24}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://uskoreainstitute.org/pdf/HeckerDenuclearizingNK.pdf|title=Denuclearizing North Korea|author=Siegfried S. Hecker|date=May–June 2008|doi=10.2968/064002011|bibcode=2008BuAtS..64b..44H|accessdate=2008-09-24|journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|volume=64|pages=44–49|issue=2|s2cid=144259915 |url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130102173916/http://uskoreainstitute.org/pdf/HeckerDenuclearizingNK.pdf|archivedate=2013-01-02}}</ref> In November 2010, Hecker visited the Yongbyon nuclear facility and reported on its advanced state.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://cisac.stanford.edu/publications/north_koreas_yongbyon_nuclear_complex_a_report_by_siegfried_s_hecker/ | author=Siegfried Hecker | title=North Korea's Yongbyon Nuclear Complex, a Report by Siegfried Hecker | date=November 20, 2010 | accessdate=November 23, 2010}}</ref> In February 2019 Hecker along with Robert L. Carlin and Elliot A. Serbin published an update to North Koreas nuclear history study saying that in 2018 North Korea "took significant steps to halt and roll back key parts of its nuclear program" and [[Kim Jong Un]] "took the extraordinary step of ending nuclear tests and missile tests, not just declaring a moratorium." in the study it also suggests the North Korea, South Korea, and the US explore cooperative efforts to demilitarize North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs and convert them to civilian nuclear and space programs.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 11, 2019 |title=Key Takeaways from 2018 update of North Korea nuclear history study |url=https://fsi-live.s3.us-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2018_colorupdate_takeawaysfin.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231120012720/https://fsi-live.s3.us-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2018_colorupdate_takeawaysfin.pdf |archive-date=20 November 2023 |access-date=20 November 2023}}</ref>

==== Memberships in organizations ====
In addition to his [[National Academy of Engineering]] (NAE) membership, Dr. Hecker is a foreign member of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] and [[Indian Institute of Metals|India Institute of Metals]]; fellow of the Minerals, Metallurgy and Materials Society (TMS), [[ASM International (society)|American Society for Metals]], [[American Physical Society]] (APS), [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS), and [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]; and honorary member of the [[American Ceramic Society|American Ceramics Society]].<ref name=":1" />

==Awards==
His achievements have been recognized with the [[American Nuclear Society]]'s [[Glenn T. Seaborg Medal|Seaborg Medal]] and many other awards including the 2018 National Engineering Award from the [[American Association of Engineering Societies]], the 2017 [[American Nuclear Society]] Eisenhower Medal, the Navy League of the U.S.'s TR & FD Roosevelt Gold Medal for Science Award in 1996, the [[AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy]], the [[Leo Szilard Lectureship Award|Leo Szilard Lectureship]] (APS), the Department of Energy's [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award|E.O. Lawrence Award]], the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|LANL]] Medal, and the [[Case Western Reserve University]] Alumni Association Gold Medal and Undergraduate Distinguished Alumni Award.<ref name=":1" />

The Secretary of Energy named Hecker, co-recipient of the 2009 [[Enrico Fermi Award]]. This Presidential Award is one of the oldest and most prestigious given by the U.S. Government and carries an honorarium of $375,000. He shares the honor with [[John Bannister Goodenough]], a professor at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].

In 2022, Hecker was an honoree by the [[Carnegie Corporation of New York]]'s [[Great Immigrants Award|Great Immigrant Award]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Siegfried S. Hecker |url=https://www.carnegie.org/awards/honoree/siegfried-hecker/ |access-date=June 12, 2024 |website=Carnegie Corporation of New York}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=University |first=© Stanford |last2=Stanford |last3=California 94305 |date=2022-06-30 |title=Dr. Siegfried Hecker named by the Carnegie Corporation of New York on its |url=https://fsi.stanford.edu/news/dr-siegfried-hecker-named-carnegie-corporation-new-york-its-annual-list-great-immigrants |access-date=2024-06-18 |website=fsi.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref>
